statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (80 trials, 29,861 people in the Cochrane living review, searched to 1 January 2026; 11 trials with 4,114 people compared with nicotine replacement and 7 trials with 1,918 people compared with vapes without nicotine; the trial supplied the vape in most), being given a nicotine vape, compared with nicotine replacement, increased the number not smoking at 6 months or longer: about 4 more people in 100 (10 against 6 in 100, interval 7 to 13; risk ratio 1.61, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.12; I² 55%); and, compared with a vape without nicotine, by about 2 more in 100 (8 against 6 in 100, interval 6 to 10; risk ratio 1.34, 1.05 to 1.69; I² 0%) (analysed as allocated, with people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). The 6 in 100 is the review's assumed quit rate with limited behavioural support, not the trials' observed rate; the risk ratios are the pooled results. Leaving out the one industry-funded trial in each comparison gave 1.72 (1.23 to 2.39) against nicotine replacement and 1.28 (1.01 to 1.64) against vapes without nicotine, and leaving out high-risk trials gave 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34) and 1.40 (1.09 to 1.81). The review rates the comparison with nicotine replacement high certainty; the editors rate it moderate, because I² is above the 50% mark the review itself calls substantial, its funnel plot is asymmetric (which the authors say could reflect unpublished small trials) and the pool has only 11 trials. How long people kept vaping could not be pooled against nicotine replacement (5 trials, I² 95%): at 6 months or longer more people in the vape group than in the nicotine replacement group were still using their allocated product in 3 trials, and there was no difference in 2. In the five trials that reported product patterns, more people in the vape groups were vaping without smoking (risk ratio 4.40, 1.27 to 15.28; I² 78%; 2,776 people), fewer were using neither cigarettes nor a vape (0.49, 0.26 to 0.91), and possibly fewer were smoking without vaping (0.76, 0.58 to 1.01, an interval that includes no difference; 4 trials; I² 83%); the review's text gives no absolute counts for these, and they are less certain than the quit rates. All participants were adults, follow-up for quitting was 6 months or longer, the trials used regulated nicotine vapes, and the review says longer-term effects are unknown. Of the 80 trials, 8 had tobacco or vaping industry support, and six review authors are authors of included trials (who state they took no part in the inclusion or risk-of-bias decisions for those trials). Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials, adults who were given a vape with nicotine were more likely to be not smoking 6 months or more later than adults given nicotine patches, gum or similar: about 10 in 100 against about 6 in 100. They also did a little better than adults given a vape without nicotine: about 8 in 100 against about 6 in 100. At the end, in 3 of 5 trials, more people given vapes were still using them than people given nicotine replacement were still using theirs. These were adults in trials where the vape was handed out, and people were followed for 6 months or more; what happens after that is not known.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (80 trials, 29,861 people in the review; 11 trials, 4,114 people against nicotine replacement; 7 trials, 1,918 people against vapes without nicotine); the vape was supplied by the trial in most; Cochrane living review, search to 1 January 2026
exposure: Being given a nicotine vape (cartridge, refillable, pod or disposable devices)
comparator: Nicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum, lozenge or combinations); a vape without nicotine
outcome: Not smoking at 6 months or longer (strictest definition, biochemically confirmed where possible, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking); still using the allocated product, vaping or smoking at that point
magnitude: Cessation at 6+ months. Vs NRT: RR 1.61 (95% CI 1.23–2.12), I² 55%, 11 trials, 4,114 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) vs 10 per 100 (7–13), about 4 more in 100 (1–7), editors' subtraction; Cochrane high, editors moderate. Vs non-nicotine vape: RR 1.34 (1.05–1.69), I² 0%, 7 trials, 1,918 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) vs 8 per 100 (6–10), about 2 more in 100 (0–4); moderate. Sensitivity: vs NRT without the industry-funded trial 1.72 (1.23–2.39), without the 2 high-risk trials 1.74 (1.30–2.34); vs non-nicotine without the industry-funded trial 1.28 (1.01–1.64), without the high-risk trial 1.40 (1.09–1.81). Use afterwards vs NRT (not graded): allocated product still in use at 6+ months not pooled (5 trials, I² 95%); vaping without smoking RR 4.40 (1.27–15.28; I² 78%; 2,776); neither vaping nor smoking RR 0.49 (0.26–0.91; I² 31%; 2,776); smoking without vaping RR 0.76 (0.58–1.01; I² 83%; 4 trials; 2,543).

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Direct comparisons between nicotine EC and other pharmacotherapies › Cessation, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings 1
evidence.extracted: Nicotine vape against NRT, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.61 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.12), I² 55%, 11 trials, 4,114 participants. Summary of findings: 6 per 100 with NRT (an assumed quit rate with limited behavioural support) against 10 per 100 (7 to 13) with a nicotine vape, about 4 more in 100 (interval 1 to 7 more; editors' subtraction). The review rates this high certainty with no downgrade. Six of the 11 trials were at low risk of bias, three unclear and two high.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Subgroup and sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (rows Analysis 1.1 and 1.2)
evidence.extracted: NRT comparison: the pregnancy trial did not differ from the rest (P = 0.89). Split by NRT type (4 trials combination NRT, 5 single-form, 2 unclear) there was little evidence of a subgroup difference (P = 0.11, I² 55.1%; P = 0.52 comparing combination with single-form only). Without the one industry-funded trial (Russell 2021) RR 1.72 (1.23 to 2.39), I² 56%; without the two high-risk trials RR 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34), I² 55%. For the combination-NRT subgroup Table 2 gives RR 1.95 (1.01 to 3.73), I² 74%, after removing high-risk trials; the main-analysis subgroup estimates are in a forest plot that was not read.

evidence.locator: Results › Reporting biases; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Synthesis methods
evidence.extracted: Six pools had 10 or more studies and five showed some asymmetry, including the NRT cessation pool (11 trials) and the behavioural-support cessation pool (11 trials). The authors say plots with this few studies are not diagnostic, that asymmetry could reflect unpublished small trials that showed no benefit or differences between trials, that they did not downgrade for publication bias and will keep monitoring. The Methods define I² above 50% as substantial; the NRT cessation pool has 55% and was not downgraded for inconsistency, while adverse events in the same comparison (72%) were.

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Versus non-nicotine, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Analysis 8.1); Summary of findings 2
evidence.extracted: Nicotine vape against non-nicotine vape, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.34 (1.05 to 1.69), I² 0%, 7 trials (five cartridge, two refillable), 1,918 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) against 8 per 100 (6 to 10), about 2 more in 100 (interval 0 to 4; editors' subtraction). Moderate certainty: not downgraded for risk of bias (one high-risk trial; without it RR 1.40, 1.09 to 1.81), one level for imprecision (fewer than 300 quits). Without the one industry-funded trial (Caponnetto 2013) RR 1.28 (1.01 to 1.64).

evidence.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Study product use; Long-term nicotine EC and combustible cigarette use
evidence.extracted: Against NRT: use of the allocated product at six months or longer was reported by 5 trials (none at high risk of bias; one, Russell 2021, industry-funded) and could not be pooled (I² 95%); in 3 trials more people in the vape arm kept using it than in the NRT arm, in 2 (Russell 2021, Lee 2018) there was no difference. Five trials (counted separately in the text: none industry-funded, one high risk) reported long-term product patterns: vaping without smoking RR 4.40 (1.27 to 15.28), I² 78%, 2,776 participants; abstinence from both vaping and smoking RR 0.49 (0.26 to 0.91), I² 31%, 2,776; concurrent vaping and smoking higher in the vape arm in 3 of 4 trials (not pooled); smoking without vaping RR 0.76 (0.58 to 1.01), I² 83%, 4 trials, 2,543. Absolute counts are in forest plots that were not read.

evidence.locator: Front matter › Funding; Results › Description of studies › Funding; Table 1; Table 2; Discussion › Limitations of the review processes; Declarations of interest; Sources of support
evidence.extracted: Funding of the 80 trials: 8 report tobacco or vaping industry support (Caponnetto 2013 and 2023, Cravo 2016, Edmiston 2022, Kanobe 2022, Rose 2023, Russell 2021, Xu 2023), 66 report none, 6 do not report. One industry-funded trial sits in each of the three cessation pools (Russell 2021 in the NRT pool, Caponnetto 2013 in the non-nicotine pool, Xu 2023 in the behavioural-support pool); removing it left each estimate positive. The review's funding comes from Cancer Research UK, NIHR infrastructure funding and, for some new outcomes, the US National Cancer Institute and FDA Center for Tobacco Products; the authors state they receive no tobacco or vaping industry funding. Six review authors are authors of included trials and state they took no part in eligibility, extraction, risk of bias or GRADE decisions for those trials.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Authors' conclusions; Methods › Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis; Results › Description of studies › Included studies › Participants; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review (including the Cessation and Adverse and serious adverse events paragraphs); Limitations of the review processes; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice and for research
evidence.extracted: Authors: imprecision remains the main limit for some comparisons; longer-term health effects are unknown and the review includes safety data to two years only; the trials tested regulated nicotine vapes, and illicit products or products containing other active substances such as THC may have different harm profiles; the field and devices change quickly and trial devices lag the market; planned subgroups by device type could not be run; unpublished data may be missing; the search ran to 1 January 2026; all trials were in adults.

imprecision.note: Nicotine against non-nicotine vape: fewer than 300 quits (review's rating moderate). Nicotine against NRT: the review rates high; the editors reach moderate by one level for I² 55% and funnel asymmetry, the same final rating.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane living review (random-effects with Hartung-Knapp intervals; AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). The claim carries the rating of its weakest link. For the comparison with vapes without nicotine the review itself gives moderate (one level for imprecision: fewer than 300 quits; not downgraded for risk of bias, as the one high-risk trial removed gives a larger estimate). For the comparison with nicotine replacement the review gives high, with no downgrade; the editors give moderate, for these reasons: I² is 55%, above the 50% line the review's own Methods call substantial (the review downgraded the adverse-event outcome of the same comparison for I² 72%); the pool's funnel plot is asymmetric, which the Discussion says may reflect publication bias or differences between trials; and with 11 trials the argument the 2018 nicotine replacement authors rely on (so many trials that smaller ones would not change the result) is not available. The editors did not add a second level, because the estimate is unchanged without the industry-funded trial or the high-risk trials and its interval stays well above no difference. The claim is therefore moderate on either route and the senior author may keep the review's high for the comparison with nicotine replacement. Risk of bias, not rated down: 6 of the 11 trials against nicotine replacement were low risk and 2 high; people could not be blinded to vape against patch or gum, but quitting was assessed with biochemical confirmation where possible. Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to adults in trials with trial-supplied, regulated vapes. The use-afterwards figures (product patterns, continued use) are not graded by the review, are heterogeneous (I² 95%, 78%, 83%) and have absolute counts only in figures that were not read; the editors regard them as low certainty and the statement labels them as less certain. One industry-funded trial sits in each pool (Russell 2021, Caponnetto 2013); results hold without them. Status replicated: the comparison with nicotine replacement and the comparison with vapes without nicotine each rest on several trials from different groups and countries; some groups contributed more than one trial and six review authors are authors of included trials. The review is a living review: later updates will change the numbers.

verification.flag_note: Staged as three claims instead of the brief's one: this one (nicotine vape against nicotine replacement and against vapes without nicotine, with how long people kept vaping), cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support (against support only or no support, low certainty) and cl_nic_vapes_harms (side effects and serious events), so that each keeps its own rating; the senior author may merge them. Certainty differs from Cochrane for the comparison with nicotine replacement (review: high; editors: moderate, reasons in the grade reasoning); the claim reads moderate either way because the non-nicotine comparison is moderate. The absolute quit rates in the review's tables are built from an assumed baseline, not observed rates. Absolute numbers still vaping or smoking at 6 months are not in the text (forest plots are images and were not read), so the use-afterwards figures are relative only. This is the sixth update of a living review: re-check at the next one. Not read: supplementary materials, forest and funnel figures, trial reports. Review authors with ties: six are authors of included trials and state they took no part in rating them (declarations on the card). No new reference is needed (lindson_2026 exists).
